stories.headline: Trump meets Qatar PM as US-Iran diplomacy stalls; G7 weighs options
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump is set to meet Qatar's prime minister at the White House, with Qatari mediation between Washington and Tehran the central agenda item as diplomacy stalls. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking before departing for a G7 foreign ministers' meeting in Paris, said Trump preferred a diplomatic solution but described Iran's demands as outrageous and ridiculous, and defended a war now more than eight months old that he conceded was not 'necessarily popular' with voters. Trump separately said fresh attacks on Iran were 'unlikely', a remark that pushed oil prices lower, while his administration said 'Task Force Iron Gate' is in full force to restrict Iranian trade routes, military supplies and revenue through coordinated land and maritime enforcement. Israel's Defence Minister Katz said the mission against Iran is 'not complete', alleging Tehran is again trying to obtain nuclear weapons. The G7 ministers' Paris meeting carries the twin agenda of ending the Ukraine conflict and halting a new Iran war.
stories.whyItMatters: West Asia instability transmits directly to India through crude supply and prices via the Strait of Hormuz, its Gulf diaspora and remittances, and its Chabahar/INSTC connectivity plans. The G7-Iran standoff also tests whether club-based crisis management can substitute for a gridlocked multilateral system — core GS-II IR and GS-III energy-security territory.

static.topic: India's West Asia policy: strategic autonomy amid the US-Iran confrontation
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India & the World (India's foreign policy, diaspora and energy interests in West Asia)
static.whatIsIt: India's approach of strategic autonomy and multi-alignment in West Asia: engaging the US, Israel and the Gulf states while retaining working ties with Iran, without joining any bloc or war.
static.background: Rooted in NAM (1961) and Panchsheel (1954); post-1991 liberalisation and the 1998 nuclear tests reshaped ties with the US, while the Indo-Pacific concept and the Quad gained salience after 2017. In West Asia, India deals simultaneously with Israel, the GCC states and Iran — Chabahar port and the INSTC are its principal connectivity anchors in Iran.
static.geography: West Asia/Persian Gulf; the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint; Chabahar on Iran's Makran coast facing the Gulf of Oman; INSTC route running via Iran and the Caspian to Russia.
static.socioEconomic: Large Indian diaspora and remittance flows from the Gulf; India's crude imports are dominated by West Asian suppliers, so higher energy prices feed inflation and the current account deficit.
static.whyInNews: The Trump-Qatar PM meeting, Rubio's remarks before the G7 Paris meeting, the 'Task Force Iron Gate' enforcement drive and Israel's 'mission not complete' statement together keep the US-Iran standoff — and its consequences for India's energy and diaspora stakes — in focus.
static.wayForward: Sustain quiet multi-alignment: keep channels to both Washington and Tehran open, diversify crude sourcing and expand strategic reserves, push Chabahar and INSTC progress, and keep consular/evacuation contingencies ready for the Gulf diaspora.
prelimsPointers: India has operated the Shahid Beheshti terminal at Iran's Chabahar port and signed a long-term contract with Iran in 2024.
The INSTC links India to Russia via Iran and the Caspian Sea, offering an alternative to the Suez route.
static.mainsAngle: Assess how India can protect its energy, connectivity and diaspora interests in West Asia while preserving strategic autonomy during a US-Iran confrontation.

static.topic: The G7 as a crisis-management club: limits of informal global governance
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance (United Nations & multilateral reform; groupings such as G7 and G20)
static.whatIsIt: The G7 is an informal grouping of seven advanced economies — US, UK, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and Canada — with the EU participating; it coordinates positions on security and economic crises but has no charter or binding authority.
static.background: It began as a G6 summit in 1975, became the G7 with Canada in 1976, and the G8 when Russia joined in 1997; Russia was suspended after the 2014 Crimea annexation. Its relative weight has declined as the G20 and BRICS grew. India has used the G20 and BRICS to press for UN Security Council reform, where the G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) campaigns for expansion, while the Intergovernmental Negotiations remain inconclusive.
static.socioEconomic: G7 decisions on sanctions and energy shape global oil prices, shipping and insurance costs and food/fertiliser prices, which are transmitted to India through trade and inflation.
static.whyInNews: G7 foreign ministers met in Paris to discuss ending the Ukraine conflict and preventing a renewed Iran war, with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio attending before the Trump-Qatar talks.
static.wayForward: India should keep engaging both the G7 and the Global South; the gap between club-based governance and universal bodies strengthens the case for UNSC reform and for India's bridging role.
prelimsPointers: G7 members are the US, UK, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and Canada; the EU attends as a non-member.
The UNSC has 15 members — 5 permanent, veto-wielding members and 10 elected for two-year terms.
static.mainsAngle: Do informal clubs like the G7 complement or undermine the UN system? Examine with reference to UNSC reform and India's claim to permanent membership.

static.topic: Strait of Hormuz: the chokepoint that decides India's oil bill
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Energy Security and Infrastructure (chokepoints, crude imports, strategic petroleum reserves)
static.whatIsIt: The Strait of Hormuz is the narrow passage connecting the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea; a very large share of seaborne crude and LNG from Gulf producers transits it.
static.background: Iran has repeatedly threatened to close the Strait during past confrontations, and disruption risks have historically spiked crude prices and shipping/insurance costs. India sources most of its crude from West Asian producers and holds strategic petroleum reserves, which is why Hormuz headlines move Indian markets.
static.geography: Narrow chokepoint between Iran to the north and Oman/the Musandam peninsula to the south, roughly 39 km wide at its narrowest, with designated inbound and outbound shipping lanes.
static.socioEconomic: Higher crude prices feed India's inflation, current account deficit and fuel pricing; disruption to Gulf shipping also affects Indian exports and the diaspora.
static.whyInNews: Reporting on the US-Iran war noted higher energy prices stemming from disruptions to shipments in the Strait of Hormuz, while oil prices fell after Trump said fresh attacks on Iran were 'unlikely'.
static.wayForward: Diversify crude sourcing, expand strategic petroleum reserves, promote rupee-based settlement and long-term supply contracts, and accelerate renewables and ethanol blending to blunt chokepoint risk.
prelimsPointers: Hormuz links the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman; Bab-el-Mandeb and the Suez Canal are the other key West Asian chokepoints.
India is among the world's largest crude importers and holds strategic petroleum reserves at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur.
static.mainsAngle: Chokepoint politics in West Asia is fundamentally an energy-security problem for India. Discuss diversification and strategic-reserve options in this light.

stories.headline: COP31 opens in Antalya as climate and geopolitical pressures mount
stories.summary: COP31 has opened in Antalya, Türkiye, with more than 100,000 participants expected over two weeks, as climate negotiations unfold amid geopolitical uncertainty. The summit is expected to produce further climate deals, but Scroll.in notes a persistent gap between target-setting and measurable outcomes. On the sidelines, the IEA chief pointed to India's renewable energy expansion as a lesson for emerging economies, while the EU moved closer to linking its carbon market with the UK's nearly six years after Brexit. Together, the developments highlight both continued multilateral engagement and the implementation challenge facing the climate regime.

static.whatIsIt: The Indian monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds driven by differential heating, the ITCZ shift, and the Tibetan Plateau's heat pump. It delivers ~75% of annual rainfall during June–September.
static.background: El Niño usually weakens the monsoon; La Niña strengthens it; the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) modulates it too. The Western Ghats and Himalayan rivers (Indus, Ganga, Brahmaputra) define drainage; peninsular rivers are rain-fed.

stories.headline: Parliament's Monsoon session stays unprorogued for record 88 days
stories.summary: Parliament's Monsoon session has not been formally prorogued, and as of the morning of 9 November 2026 both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha remained technically alive 88 days after the session began — the longest such stretch on record. Because prorogation is the step that formally ends a session, the existing session can be reconvened for an extended sitting without a fresh summons being issued. The development turns attention to India's parliamentary calendar, which rests on Article 85 and on convention rather than on any statutory schedule. It also raises questions about how session management affects the planning and scrutiny of pending legislative business.
stories.whyItMatters: Tests understanding of Article 85, the distinction between adjournment, prorogation and dissolution, and how the timing of sessions shapes legislative scrutiny — a recurring GS-II theme.

perspectives.take: Reports the 88-day unprorogued stretch as a record and frames it around the procedural possibility of convening an extended sitting of the existing session; a straight news report without evident editorial slant.

static.topic: Prorogation of Parliament and the Session Cycle
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Parliament & Legislative Process
static.whatIsIt: Prorogation is the formal termination of a session of Parliament by the President under Article 85, acting on the advice of the Council of Ministers. It ends the session but not the life of the House; a fresh summons is required to convene the next session.
static.background: Article 85 provides that the President summons each House, may prorogue it, and may dissolve the Lok Sabha, and that not more than six months may intervene between two sessions. Adjournment, ordered by the presiding officer, only suspends a sitting; prorogation ends the whole session; dissolution ends the House itself. Pending Bills survive prorogation, but pending notices, motions and other business lapse.
static.whyInNews: As of 9 November 2026, neither House had been prorogued, leaving the Monsoon session formally alive for a record 88 days and permitting an extended sitting to be convened without fresh summons.
static.wayForward: Move towards a published, predictable parliamentary calendar so that session dates and prorogation are known in advance, reducing uncertainty over legislative business.
prelimsPointers: Article 85: the President summons and prorogues the Houses; the maximum gap between two sessions is six months.
Prorogation ends the session; pending Bills do not lapse, but pending notices and motions do.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how the timing of prorogation and the session calendar affect legislative scrutiny and executive accountability.

static.topic: Ordinance-making power (Article 123)
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Executive & Legislative Relations
static.whatIsIt: Article 123 allows the President to promulgate Ordinances at a time when both Houses of Parliament are not in session, giving them the force of law; every Ordinance must be laid before Parliament and ceases to operate six weeks after reassembly unless approved.
static.background: Ordinances are co-extensive with Parliament's legislative competence and are subject to judicial review. Courts have held that repeated re-promulgation of Ordinances is a fraud on the Constitution and that Ordinances must be laid before the legislature.
static.whyInNews: An unprorogued session keeps Parliament formally in session, which bears on the constitutional condition under which Ordinances may be promulgated.
static.wayForward: Reserve Ordinances for genuinely urgent needs and replace them with regular legislation within the stipulated period.
prelimsPointers: An Ordinance must be approved by Parliament within six weeks of its reassembly.
Re-promulgation of Ordinances has been held to be a fraud on the Constitution.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether frequent recourse to Ordinances undermines parliamentary deliberation.

stories.headline: Supreme Court green cracker window in focus as NCR air quality worsens
stories.summary: The Supreme Court allowed the bursting of only certified green firecrackers in Delhi-NCR on November 7 and 8, 2026, within two windows — 6 a.m. to 7 a.m. and 8 p.m. to 10 p.m. The directions were issued amid worsening winter air quality in the National Capital Region, with the court-appointed amicus curiae telling the bench that the lungs of even Delhi's children are no longer healthy. Coverage of the order has focused on the permitted time slots and green-cracker certification norms, but also on the persistent gap between judicial directions and their enforcement on the ground. The episode sits within a longer judicial effort to regulate firecracker use and air pollution through continuing orders rather than a single verdict.
stories.whyItMatters: It illustrates the Supreme Court's use of PIL and Article 32 jurisdiction to regulate environmental and public-health matters, and raises the enduring question of judicial directives versus executive enforcement capacity.

static.topic: Supreme Court, PIL and Judicial Review in Environmental Governance
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary: judicial review, PIL, enforcement of fundamental rights
static.whatIsIt: The Supreme Court (Article 124) is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution, with writ jurisdiction under Article 32; High Courts exercise parallel power under Article 214 and Article 226. Judicial review lets courts test executive action and laws against the Constitution, and PILs allow any public-spirited person to approach the court on behalf of affected groups — the route through which pollution and firecracker regulation has largely been litigated.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998); Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine; PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s. Environmental litigation followed the same arc, with courts reading the right to a clean environment into Article 21 and issuing continuing mandamus — a series of monitoring orders rather than a one-time decree. Firecracker regulation in Delhi-NCR has been handled through this continuing-order route, with the Supreme Court mandating green crackers and time windows and relying on court-appointed amicus curiae for ground feedback.
static.geography: Delhi-NCR sits in the Indo-Gangetic plain; winter temperature inversion, low wind speed and a shallow mixing height trap particulate matter, compounded by stubble burning in Punjab and Haryana and local vehicular and industrial emissions.
static.socioEconomic: The firecracker industry, concentrated in Sivakasi in Tamil Nadu, supports large numbers of informal workers, so bans and certification requirements carry livelihood consequences; conversely, the health burden of particulate exposure falls disproportionately on children, the elderly and outdoor workers.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court permitted certified green firecrackers in Delhi-NCR only between 6 a.m. and 7 a.m. and between 8 p.m. and 10 p.m. on November 7 and 8, 2026, with the amicus curiae flagging the deteriorating lung health of Delhi's children.
static.wayForward: Strengthen source apportionment and real-time monitoring, build enforcement capacity at the municipal level, provide a transition package for firecracker workers, and pursue coordinated regional action across NCR states rather than city-limited measures.
prelimsPointers: Original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court lies in disputes between the Centre and states under Article 131; advisory jurisdiction is under Article 143.
Writ jurisdiction: Article 32 for the Supreme Court, Article 226 for High Courts — Article 226 is wider in scope.
Green crackers are a certified category developed to reduce particulate and sound emissions, using alternative chemicals instead of barium-based formulations.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether continuing judicial mandates on air pollution strengthen environmental governance or expose the limits of judicial enforcement in the absence of executive capacity.

static.topic: Delhi-NCR Air Pollution Governance and the Graded Response Action Plan
static.syllabusNode: Environment — pollution: air quality management, institutional mechanisms
static.whatIsIt: Air quality in Delhi-NCR is managed through a statutory framework anchored in the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, and, since 2021, a dedicated regional authority for the NCR and adjoining areas. The Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) escalates restrictions — on construction, transport, industry and waste burning — in stages as air quality deteriorates.
static.background: GRAP was first notified in 2017 on Supreme Court directions and was revised subsequently to introduce pre-defined, graded stages triggered by Air Quality Index thresholds. The regional authority for NCR and adjoining areas was set up in 2021 by an Act of Parliament to coordinate across Delhi, Haryana, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh, superseding earlier ad hoc coordination arrangements.
static.geography: The NCR spans the Gangetic plain, where winter meteorology — temperature inversion, calm winds and low mixing height — traps pollutants close to the ground, while transboundary stubble burning adds to local emissions.
static.socioEconomic: Pollution episodes impose measurable health costs, school closures, restrictions on construction and transport that affect informal livelihoods, and a disproportionate burden on low-income households with limited access to clean fuels and healthcare.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court's green-cracker windows for November 7-8, 2026 were issued against the backdrop of worsening NCR air quality and submissions on the health impact on children.
static.wayForward: Move from episodic emergency restrictions to year-round source reduction — cleaner fuels, public transport expansion, waste-management reform, mechanised crop-residue management and credible emissions monitoring.

prelimsPointers: GRAP is a graded set of anti-pollution measures that tighten as air quality worsens, applied across Delhi-NCR.
A dedicated statutory authority for air quality management in NCR and adjoining areas was created in 2021 to coordinate across the concerned states.
static.mainsAngle: Assess the effectiveness of GRAP and the regional air-quality authority in tackling winter pollution in Delhi-NCR, and suggest institutional reforms to shift policy from crisis response to sustained source reduction.

stories.headline: Nvidia board probes whether CEO Huang was targeted by Chinese intelligence
stories.summary: Nvidia's board has opened an investigation into whether CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by Chinese intelligence, after Huang acknowledged to the board that he had been intimate with a business executive whom U.S. intelligence had assessed as gathering information for Beijing. The company disclosed the probe amid heightened scrutiny of its China business, national security concerns and open questions about leadership succession at the world's most valuable chip designer. President Donald Trump publicly urged Huang to remain in his role, signalling political backing even as the board inquiry proceeds. The episode sits at the intersection of great-power technology rivalry, corporate governance and counter-intelligence, and has drawn wide coverage across U.S. and Indian outlets.
stories.whyItMatters: It illustrates how semiconductor leadership has become a national-security asset, making corporate espionage, export controls and CEO succession questions in chip firms directly relevant to US–China strategic competition and to India's own chip ambitions.

static.topic: India Semiconductor Mission and chip supply-chain resilience
static.syllabusNode: Science & Technology — Indigenisation of technology; Economy — Industrial policy and infrastructure
static.whatIsIt: The India Semiconductor Mission (ISM), launched under MeitY in December 2021 with an outlay of about ₹76,000 crore, is the umbrella programme to build a domestic semiconductor and display manufacturing ecosystem. It supports four pillars: silicon fabs, ATMP/OSAT (assembly, testing, marking, packaging) units, display fabs, and design-linked incentives for fabless startups.
static.background: Announced alongside the Semicon India programme, ISM followed decades of largely unsuccessful attempts to attract wafer fabrication to India. From 2023–24, approvals were announced for an ATMP unit by Micron in Sanand (Gujarat), a fab in Dholera (Gujarat) and an OSAT unit in Morigaon district, Assam. The programme is complemented by the Design Linked Incentive scheme and state-level semiconductor policies.
static.geography: Key nodes include Dholera and Sanand in Gujarat and Jagiroad/Morigaon in Assam; the wider ecosystem depends on imported equipment, chemicals and ultra-pure water infrastructure.
static.socioEconomic: Semiconductor manufacturing is capital-intensive but generates high-skill employment, reduces India's import bill for electronics components, and anchors downstream electronics and automotive value chains.
static.whyInNews: The Nvidia probe highlights how advanced chip design and AI accelerator supply are concentrated in a handful of firms, making the geopolitics of semiconductors a live national-security issue — the same logic that drives India's push for domestic fabrication.
static.wayForward: Sustained policy stability, talent pipelines in VLSI design, reliable power and water infrastructure, and partnerships with global foundries are needed to move from assembly to leading-edge fabrication.
prelimsPointers: ISM was launched in December 2021 under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology with an outlay of about ₹76,000 crore.
ATMP stands for Assembly, Testing, Marking and Packaging — the back-end of the chip value chain, typically the first stage India has attracted.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how far India's semiconductor incentive architecture addresses the structural constraints — capital, water, power and skilled manpower — that have historically deterred wafer fabrication.

static.topic: US–China strategic technology rivalry and semiconductor export controls
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Effect of policies and politics of developed and developing countries on India's interests
static.whatIsIt: A set of US measures restricting the export of advanced semiconductors, chipmaking equipment and related technology to China, aimed at slowing Chinese advances in AI and military computing. Implemented through export control rules, the Entity List and the Foreign Direct Product Rule.
static.background: Broad controls were announced in October 2022 and tightened in October 2023, covering advanced logic and memory chips and lithography equipment. The US aligned the Netherlands and Japan on equipment restrictions. China responded with export curbs on gallium and germanium and later on graphite. The US CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 subsidised domestic fabrication.
static.geography: Centres on East Asia's fabrication clusters — Taiwan, South Korea, Japan — and on US-allied equipment suppliers in the Netherlands and Japan.
static.socioEconomic: Controls raise costs and fragment supply chains, pushing firms to build 'China-plus-one' capacity; they also create market-access uncertainty for firms such as Nvidia that design China-specific compliant chips.
static.whyInNews: The Nvidia board probe has intensified scrutiny of the company's China exposure at a time when Washington treats advanced computing as a security domain rather than a purely commercial one.
static.wayForward: For India, the opportunity lies in becoming a trusted supply-chain partner under frameworks such as the US–India initiative on Critical and Emerging Technology, while avoiding being drawn into binary bloc politics.
prelimsPointers: The US CHIPS and Science Act was enacted in 2022 to subsidise domestic semiconductor manufacturing and research.
China imposed export controls on gallium and germanium in 2023 — both critical for chipmaking and optoelectronics.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how US–China semiconductor export controls affect India's strategic autonomy and its prospects of integrating into global chip value chains.

static.topic: Economic espionage, counter-intelligence and national security
static.syllabusNode: Internal Security — Security challenges and their management; linkages of organised crime with terrorism; basics of cyber security
static.whatIsIt: Economic espionage is state-sponsored or state-directed collection of sensitive commercial, technical or proprietary information. In the United States it is prosecuted principally under the Economic Espionage Act, 1996, alongside counter-intelligence investigations by the FBI.
static.background: The US has pursued high-profile economic espionage and sanctions cases involving foreign firms and researchers over the past decade. Counter-intelligence concerns have expanded from defence secrets to dual-use technologies such as AI, semiconductors and biotechnology. India's legal framework rests on the Official Secrets Act, 1923, the Atomic Energy Act and IT Act provisions, with coordination through the National Security Council Secretariat.
static.socioEconomic: Loss of intellectual property raises research and development costs, erodes first-mover advantage and can distort competition in strategic industries.
static.whyInNews: The reported assessment that a business executive close to Nvidia's CEO was gathering information for Beijing has revived debate on how private technology firms manage counter-intelligence risk.
static.wayForward: Firms handling strategic technology need robust personnel vetting, insider-threat programmes and clear disclosure norms, while states must balance security screening against privacy and due process.
prelimsPointers: The US Economic Espionage Act of 1996 criminalises theft of trade secrets for the benefit of a foreign government.
India's Official Secrets Act, 1923 remains the principal statute governing espionage and disclosure of sensitive information.
static.mainsAngle: As strategic technologies move into private hands, examine whether India's counter-intelligence architecture is equipped to protect commercial intellectual property in the semiconductor and AI sectors.

stories.headline: Khor Mor gas field hit by drone; Indian seafarers evacuated from Yemen
stories.summary: Production at Iraq's Khor Mor gas field was suspended after a drone attack, with an engineer at the site reporting that a gas storage facility was struck and crew were moved into shelters amid fears of further strikes. Separately, India's embassy in Yemen said 19 Indian seafarers stranded there had been evacuated, days after New Delhi confirmed that 14 Indians aboard a yacht involved in an incident off the Yemeni coast were safe. The incidents unfold against escalating fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, with a Syrian official saying an initial force of about 600 Syrian special forces personnel is expected to deploy to Saudi Arabia in the coming week. Together the developments underline how West Asian instability is now simultaneously a supply-side energy risk and a direct consular-protection challenge for India.
stories.whyItMatters: West Asia supplies a large share of India's crude and LPG, and hosts a diaspora of millions — so any escalation there feeds directly into energy security, shipping costs and consular obligations, all recurring UPSC themes.

perspectives.take: Frames the Khor Mor strike through on-the-ground impact — storage facility hit, crew sheltering — emphasising operational disruption at the field.

static.topic: West Asia instability and India's energy security
static.syllabusNode: Infrastructure: Energy — security of supply, import dependence
static.whatIsIt: India imports a majority of its crude oil and a substantial part of its natural gas/LPG from West Asia, making the region's security environment a direct determinant of domestic energy prices and supply stability.
static.background: India's import dependence rose sharply after the 1990s liberalisation of the hydrocarbon sector. Periodic shocks — the 1990-91 Gulf War, the 2003 Iraq war, the 2011 Libyan conflict, and post-2023 Red Sea shipping disruptions — have each prompted India to diversify sourcing (West Africa, US, Latin America, Russia) and to build strategic petroleum reserves at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur.
static.geography: Khor Mor is a gas field in the Kurdistan Region of northern Iraq; Iraq sits atop some of the world's largest proven oil reserves, and its northern gas is largely used for domestic power generation.
static.socioEconomic: Higher landed fuel costs transmit into inflation, subsidy burdens and power tariffs; disruption also affects Indian construction and energy-sector workers employed in the region.
static.whyInNews: A drone attack halted production at Iraq's Khor Mor gas field, illustrating how non-state or asymmetric attacks can knock out energy infrastructure in a region India depends on.
static.wayForward: Deepen import-source diversification, expand strategic reserves, accelerate domestic renewables and gas-grid expansion, and strengthen maritime/energy-supply contingency planning.
prelimsPointers: India's strategic petroleum reserves are located at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur.
Iraq is among India's major crude suppliers, alongside Saudi Arabia, UAE, Russia and the US.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how recurring West Asian instability shapes India's energy security calculus and evaluate the adequacy of India's diversification and reserve strategies.

static.topic: India's evacuation operations and diaspora protection abroad
static.syllabusNode: Government policies and interventions; Indian diaspora
static.whatIsIt: India periodically mounts named evacuation missions to bring back nationals from conflict or crisis zones, coordinated by the Ministry of External Affairs through embassies, with Indian Armed Forces and Air India/private carriers providing lift.
static.background: Major operations include Operation Sukoon (Lebanon, 2006), Operation Safe Homecoming (Libya, 2011), Operation Raahat (Yemen, 2015), Operation Ganga (Ukraine, 2022), Operation Kaveri (Sudan, 2023) and Operation Ajay (Israel, 2023). The 2015 Yemen evacuation was notable for combining naval and airlift assets from Djibouti.
static.geography: Yemen sits at the southern tip of the Arabian Peninsula, flanking the Bab-el-Mandeb strait — a chokepoint on the Suez–Red Sea–Gulf of Aden route.
static.socioEconomic: India's West Asian diaspora is a major source of remittances; their safety is both a welfare and a foreign-policy concern.
static.whyInNews: Nineteen Indian seafarers stranded in Yemen were evacuated, days after India said 14 Indians aboard a yacht involved in an incident off the Yemeni coast were safe.
static.wayForward: Strengthen early-warning and registration mechanisms for nationals in conflict zones, pre-position evacuation logistics, and institutionalise coordination between MEA, Navy and shipping regulators.

static.wayForward: Sustain Indian Navy presence and escort operations, deepen information-sharing with regional navies, and diversify trade routes and insurance arrangements.

Red Sea diversions around the Cape of Good Hope add substantial distance and cost to Asia–Europe voyages.

stories.headline: Eisenkot gets mandate to form Israeli government, challenges Netanyahu
stories.summary: Israeli President Isaac Herzog has handed Gadi Eisenkot, 66, a former military chief turned relative political novice, the mandate to form a government after the election left no bloc with a clear majority. Eisenkot, who has promised to bridge Israel's deep polarisation under Benjamin Netanyahu, has 28 days — extendable by 14 — to assemble a coalition, and has publicly invited Netanyahu's party to join a 'wide' government under his leadership. He warned that Israel faces a crisis if the political deadlock is not resolved. Some reports describe the window as six weeks, reflecting the statutory 28-day mandate plus a possible 14-day extension. The path to power remains uncertain, since his bloc lacks a stable majority and coalition arithmetic is still fluid.
stories.whyItMatters: Who forms Israel's next government shapes West Asia diplomacy, post-conflict arrangements and India's bilateral defence, technology and connectivity engagements. It is also a live case study of coalition formation under proportional representation, a recurring UPSC theme.

static.topic: Israel's Parliamentary System and Coalition Government
static.syllabusNode: Polity & Governance — Comparison of constitutional schemes; International Relations — political systems
static.whatIsIt: Israel is a parliamentary republic with a 120-member unicameral Knesset elected by nationwide proportional representation; governments are always coalitions and no single party has ever won an outright majority.
static.background: Israel's Basic Laws function in place of a single written constitution. The President, a largely ceremonial head of state, consults parties after elections and assigns the mandate to form a government, conventionally to the candidate with the best chance of commanding the Knesset.
static.geography: Israel lies on the eastern Mediterranean, bordered by Lebanon, Syria, Jordan and Egypt, with Jerusalem as its declared capital — a status contested internationally.
static.socioEconomic: Coalition fragility reflects deep cleavages — religious versus secular, Haredi conscription, judicial powers and cost of living — that shape every government's stability.
static.whyInNews: President Isaac Herzog assigned Gadi Eisenkot the mandate to form a government after the election left no bloc with a clear majority.
static.wayForward: Watch whether a 'wide' unity government or a narrow coalition emerges; the 28-day mandate plus a possible 14-day extension is the operative deadline.
prelimsPointers: The Knesset has 120 members; Israel has no single written constitution but a set of Basic Laws.
The President assigns the mandate to form government; the Prime Minister must retain the Knesset's confidence.
static.mainsAngle: Compare coalition formation under Israel's proportional system with India's anti-defection and floor-test framework.

static.geography: Israel's position at the junction of the Mediterranean and West Asia gives it strategic salience for India's energy, trade and connectivity interests.
static.socioEconomic: Defence hardware, agri-tech and innovation partnerships are the mainstays; India simultaneously balances ties with Arab states and Iran.
static.whyInNews: A change of government in Israel could affect the pace of bilateral defence and technology cooperation and India's regional balancing.
static.wayForward: India should keep ties de-hyphenated from its Palestine and Gulf relationships and continue institutionalised dialogue.

stories.headline: UK Hindu family moves High Court over school's tilak objection
stories.summary: The parents of a nine-year-old Hindu boy have approached the UK High Court alleging religious discrimination after a London school objected to their son wearing the tilak-chandlo on its premises. The family contends that preventing the child from wearing the mark infringes his right to manifest his religion, while the school's objection is reported to rest on its uniform and institutional-neutrality rules. The matter is now before the High Court, where it will test how far schools in the UK must accommodate religious symbols. The dispute has drawn wide attention in India because it echoes domestic debates over religious markers in educational institutions.
stories.whyItMatters: It is a live test of how liberal democracies reconcile institutional neutrality with minority religious practice — the same tension Indian courts address through the essential religious practices doctrine under Articles 25–28.

static.topic: Freedom of Religion and the Essential Religious Practices Test
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Fundamental Rights (Freedom of Religion, Articles 25–28)
static.whatIsIt: Articles 25–28 guarantee freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion, subject to public order, morality and health. Courts decide what is protected by asking whether a practice is 'essential' or integral to the religion.
static.background: The essential religious practices test was laid down by the Supreme Court in Shirur Mutt (1954), which held that what is essential to a religion enjoys protection. The doctrine was expanded and contested in later cases, including the Sabarimala judgment (2018), and continues to be debated for giving courts a wide role in defining religious practice.
static.whyInNews: A UK-based Hindu family has moved the UK High Court alleging religious discrimination after a London school objected to their nine-year-old son wearing the tilak-chandlo.
prelimsPointers: Articles 25–28 cover freedom of religion; Article 25 is available to all persons, not only citizens.
The 'essential religious practices' test was laid down in Shirur Mutt (1954).
static.mainsAngle: Examine how the essential religious practices doctrine balances religious freedom against state regulation, and whether a 'reasonable accommodation' framework would be more consistent with constitutional pluralism.

static.topic: Judicial Review and Writ Jurisdiction
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary (Supreme Court, High Courts and Judicial Review)
static.whatIsIt: Judicial review is the power of courts to test executive action and legislation against the Constitution. The Supreme Court (Article 124) is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution; High Courts (Article 214) sit at the state level, and writ jurisdiction lies under Articles 32 and 226.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine. PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s.
static.whyInNews: The tilak dispute has been taken to the High Court in the UK — a reminder that superior courts are the forum where claims of religious freedom against institutions are ultimately adjudicated. India's analogue is writ jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226.
prelimsPointers: Original jurisdiction: disputes between the Centre and states (Article 131).
Advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is under Article 143.
static.mainsAngle: Examine judicial backlog, vacancies and pendency, and the balance between judicial independence and accountability.

static.topic: Indian Diaspora and Multicultural Integration
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Effect of policies of developed countries on India's interests; Indian Diaspora
static.whatIsIt: The overseas Indian community of NRIs and Persons of Indian Origin is among the world's largest diasporas. Its integration into host societies raises questions of religious accommodation, cultural identity and minority rights.
static.background: Indian emigration spans the nineteenth-century indenture system, post-independence professional migration to the UK, the US and the Gulf, and the creation of a dedicated diaspora-engagement framework. Pravasi Bharatiya Divas has been observed since 2003, and the erstwhile Ministry of Overseas Indian Affairs was merged into the Ministry of External Affairs in 2016.
static.geography: United Kingdom — home to a long-settled Indian-origin population; the present case is before a London court.
static.socioEconomic: Second- and third-generation diaspora families increasingly litigate questions of religious and cultural accommodation in schools and workplaces rather than settling them informally.
static.whyInNews: A Hindu family in the UK has gone to the High Court after a London school objected to their son wearing the tilak-chandlo.
static.wayForward: Clearer school uniform and dress policies on religious accommodation, backed by community dialogue, can reduce recourse to litigation and ease integration.
prelimsPointers: OCI cardholders are foreign nationals of Indian origin and do not enjoy voting rights in India.
Pravasi Bharatiya Divas has been observed since 2003 to engage the diaspora.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how host-country policies on religious accommodation shape the integration of the Indian diaspora and, in turn, India's soft power.

stories.headline: India's 100th chess Grandmaster, CBSE exam surge, and science briefs
stories.summary: Anuj Shrivatri became India's 100th chess Grandmaster, a milestone that caps the country's rapid expansion in elite chess. In education, the CBSE has notified timetables for the 2027 Class 10 and 12 board examinations with more than 46 lakh candidates expected, even as central universities and institutes continue to function without permanent vice-chancellors and directors because of appointment delays. On the health and science front, a new urine-based test was reported to detect about 95% of bladder cancer cases in a study, a doctor described reversing his father's diabetes, and food-safety enforcement was reported to be hobbled by staff shortages. Elsewhere, NASA's Swift observatory burned up on re-entry, underscoring the difficulty of servicing ageing satellites, Samsung's US chip plant moved towards a December trial run, and commentators examined women's participation in AI and the biology of pubic hair.
stories.whyItMatters: UPSC repeatedly tests institutional capacity — examination boards, university leadership, food-safety regulators and health-research translation — alongside India's growing strengths in sport and space. The mix also illustrates how governance, science and society stories are interlinked in the daily news cycle.

static.topic: Satellite servicing, orbital debris and India's space programme
static.syllabusNode: Science & Technology — Space Technology; Awareness in the fields of IT, Space
static.whatIsIt: Space-based assets — communication, remote sensing, navigation and scientific satellites — need periodic orbit maintenance; when fuel runs out or servicing fails, satellites re-enter and burn up, adding to orbital debris.
static.background: ISRO (1969) runs India's space programme under the Department of Space. Aryabhata (1975) was India's first satellite; Mangalyaan reached Mars orbit in 2013; Chandrayaan-3 soft-landed near the lunar south pole in 2023; Gaganyaan is India's first crewed mission. IN-SPACe (2020) and NSIL now promote private participation. NASA's Swift observatory has now burned up on re-entry, highlighting the difficulty of boosting or servicing ageing satellites.
static.socioEconomic: Space services underpin telecom, weather forecasting, disaster management and precision agriculture; debris threatens the long-term sustainability of low-Earth orbit.
static.whyInNews: NASA's Swift observatory burned up on re-entry, drawing attention to the challenges of satellite boosting and in-orbit servicing.
static.wayForward: Strengthen space situational awareness, debris mitigation and in-orbit servicing capabilities; expand IN-SPACe/NSIL-led private participation and support international space-governance norms.
prelimsPointers: PSLV is India's workhorse launcher; GSLV Mk-III can carry heavier geosynchronous payloads.
UN COPUOS governs space law; India is a founder of the Outer Space Treaty framework.
static.mainsAngle: Commercialisation of space, space debris and India's role in space governance.

static.topic: School boards and university leadership: capacity gaps in Indian education

static.whatIsIt: CBSE conducts board examinations for Classes 10 and 12, while central universities and centrally funded institutions are headed by vice-chancellors and directors appointed through statutory processes.
static.background: The Right to Education Act, 2009 guarantees free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14; the National Education Policy 2020 proposes structural reform of school and higher education. Central universities are governed under the Central Universities Act, 2009, with the President as Visitor, and UGC is the higher-education regulator. Prolonged vacancies in vice-chancellor and director posts have been reported at central institutions.
static.socioEconomic: Board examination logistics affect over 46 lakh candidates; leadership vacancies delay academic appointments, accreditation and reform implementation.
static.whyInNews: CBSE released the 2027 Class 10 and 12 timetable with over 46 lakh expected candidates, while central institutions were reported to be running without permanent vice-chancellors and directors.
static.wayForward: Time-bound, transparent appointment processes; strengthened board examination logistics and assessment reform; linking institutional funding to governance benchmarks.
prelimsPointers: The RTE Act, 2009 covers children aged 6–14; NEP 2020 replaced the 1986 policy framework.
The President of India is the Visitor of central universities.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how leadership vacancies and examination logistics affect the quality and credibility of India's education system.

static.topic: Health research translation, food safety and regulatory capacity

static.whatIsIt: India's health system combines publicly financed insurance and primary care with a regulatory apparatus covering drugs, food safety and medical research.
static.background: Ayushman Bharat (2018) has a health-insurance arm (PM-JAY) and Health & Wellness Centres; POSHAN Abhiyaan targets malnutrition. static.whyInNews: A urine test for bladder cancer, a doctor's account of reversing his father's diabetes, and reports of food-safety staff shortages together spotlight health research and regulatory capacity.
static.wayForward: Fill regulatory and inspection vacancies, strengthen laboratory networks, and build a transparent pathway from validated research to clinical and public-health practice.
prelimsPointers: Ayushman Bharat (2018) has two arms: PM-JAY insurance and Health & Wellness Centres.
FSSAI is the apex food-safety regulator under the FSS Act, 2006.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how regulatory and research-translation capacity determines health outcomes in India.

stories.headline: World briefs: US midterms fallout, Trump investigations, Pope in Argentina
stories.summary: In a week dominated by US politics, President Donald Trump told CBS's '60 Minutes' that his deportation policy had been 'too tough', while he and his Justice Department stood defiant against Democratic plans for an investigative blitz, with Trump calling their requests 'extortion at the highest level'. Republican losses in the midterms have triggered open recrimination inside MAGA ranks, with loyalists questioning his role in the setbacks. Separately, Trump dismissed as a joke his suggestion that UFC chief Dana White become White House press secretary — a post still vacant — and said he expects to meet Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin at the APEC summit in China. Former President Joe Biden said his cancer treatment is limiting his daily activities and will curtail promotion of his forthcoming memoir. Abroad, Pope Leo used a visit to a divided Argentina to press for care of the poor, pensioners and people with disabilities — read as a veiled rebuke of President Javier Milei's cuts — while Paraguayan police raided the home of former President Santiago Pena over allegations involving Ueno Bank; in the Gulf, UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed issued Diwali greetings even as conservative activists disrupted Diwali celebrations in Seattle with anti-Hindu slogans.
stories.whyItMatters: US domestic turbulence — midterm reversals, contested immigration enforcement and executive-legislative confrontation — directly shapes India's diaspora, trade and strategic calculus, while the Pope's Argentina visit and the APEC summitry signal show how welfare politics and great-power diplomacy now intersect.

static.topic: US Midterm Elections and Divided Government
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Effect of policies and politics of developed countries on India's interests
static.whatIsIt: Midterm elections are held midway through a US President's four-year term, when all 435 House seats and about a third of the 100 Senate seats are contested; they often produce divided government, in which the President's party loses ground in Congress.

stories.headline: Karnataka tests petrol at 67 sites after ethanol blending complaints
stories.summary: Karnataka has ordered petrol quality testing at 67 locations across the State following public complaints linked to ethanol-blended fuel, with Chief Minister Shivakumar stating that samples were drawn not only at retail petrol pumps but also at the ethanol blending and distribution stages of the supply chain. The move signals a widening of scrutiny beyond the retail nozzle to the entire blending-to-dispensing chain, where quality deviations are most likely to originate. The complaints come amid the nationwide scale-up of ethanol blending in petrol, which has raised concerns among motorists about vehicle performance, fuel efficiency and component compatibility. The State's inspection exercise is essentially a consumer-protection and quality-assurance response, and its findings will feed into the larger national debate on how fast blending can be expanded without compromising fuel standards.
stories.whyItMatters: Ethanol blending sits at the intersection of India's energy security, sugar and grain economics, and environmental commitments — a recurring GS-III theme. The Karnataka episode also tests federal coordination, since fuel quality standards and blending mandates are set centrally while enforcement and consumer grievance redressal play out in the States.

perspectives.take: Frames the story as a State government quality-assurance and consumer-grievance response, foregrounding the CM's statement that inspections covered blending and distribution stages, not just retail pumps — a governance-accountability angle rather than an energy-policy critique.

static.topic: Ethanol Blended Petrol (EBP) Programme
static.syllabusNode: Infrastructure: Energy — government policies and interventions; conservation and environmental pollution
static.whatIsIt: A central programme under which ethanol produced from sugarcane molasses, sugar syrup, damaged food grains, surplus rice and maize is blended with petrol by Oil Marketing Companies, with blending percentages rising in a phased manner towards E20 (20% ethanol, 80% petrol).
static.background: The EBP Programme was launched in 2003 and ethanol blending began on a pilot basis in 2006, initially confined to a few States and later extended nationwide. Blending levels rose gradually from around 1-2% in the early years to double digits in the 2020s. The National Policy on Biofuels, 2018 set an indicative target of 20% blending by 2030; this was subsequently advanced to Ethanol Supply Year 2025-26, with the government announcing the availability of E20 fuel across the country ahead of that timeline. A Parliamentary Standing Committee on Petroleum and Natural Gas examined the programme and flagged concerns over vehicle compatibility, fuel efficiency and the food-versus-fuel trade-off.
static.geography: Ethanol supply is concentrated in sugar-producing States such as Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and Karnataka, while blending and dispensing infrastructure is spread across the country — creating logistical and quality-control challenges along the chain.
static.socioEconomic: Blending supports sugarcane farmers and distillery revenues, reduces the crude oil import bill and foreign exchange outflow, and lowers tailpipe emissions of some pollutants; critics point to diversion of food grains and cane, pressure on water resources, and a possible drop in fuel efficiency for consumers.
static.whyInNews: Karnataka ordered petrol sample testing at 67 locations after complaints about ethanol-blended fuel, with inspections extended to blending and distribution stages.
static.wayForward: Strengthen end-to-end quality monitoring from distilleries to retail outlets, publish transparent test results, ensure vehicle compatibility through clear labelling and manufacturer advisories, and balance feedstock use so that food and feed security are not compromised.
prelimsPointers: E20 denotes a blend of 20% ethanol and 80% petrol by volume.
BIS standard IS 17021:2018 specifies requirements for E20 fuel for automotive spark-ignition engines.
The EBP Programme is administered by the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas through the Oil Marketing Companies.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether the accelerated push towards E20 is compatible with consumer interest, vehicle technology readiness and food security, and suggest safeguards.

static.topic: Fuel quality regulation and consumer protection in petroleum retailing
static.syllabusNode: Governance — government policies and interventions; statutory and regulatory bodies; consumer protection
static.whatIsIt: The framework of standards, testing and enforcement that ensures petrol and diesel sold to consumers meet prescribed specifications, covering BIS fuel standards, Legal Metrology requirements on quantity, and OMC quality-control mechanisms at terminals, depots and retail outlets.
static.background: Fuel specifications in India are notified by the central government and enforced through BIS standards and OMC quality checks, with periodic surprise inspections of retail outlets. Consumer complaints about adulteration or off-spec fuel have historically been handled through OMC grievance systems and State-level enforcement, and penalties can include fines, suspension of supply and cancellation of dealership. The entry of ethanol blending added a new variable to quality assurance, since blending must be done to specification and the blended product must be stored and transported without moisture ingress or phase separation.
static.socioEconomic: Off-spec or improperly blended fuel imposes direct costs on consumers through poor mileage and possible engine damage, and erodes trust in the fuel retail network; small dealers can face disproportionate penalties if upstream blending or logistics are at fault.
static.whyInNews: Karnataka's inspections at 67 locations, covering blending and distribution stages as well as retail pumps, highlight the enforcement dimension of fuel quality in the ethanol-blending era.
static.wayForward: Adopt a chain-of-custody approach with traceable batch testing, publish inspection outcomes in the public domain, fix accountability at the blending and logistics stage rather than only at the retail outlet, and provide a fast, accessible grievance redressal route for motorists.
prelimsPointers: Fuel quality standards in India are set centrally and enforced through BIS specifications and OMC inspections.
Ethanol blending must meet prescribed specifications; moisture ingress can cause phase separation in blended petrol.
Retail outlet licences can be suspended or cancelled for selling off-spec fuel.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how regulatory enforcement must adapt when a new component such as ethanol is introduced into an existing fuel supply chain.

prelims: Karnataka carried out petrol sample testing at 67 locations following complaints related to ethanol blending, as stated by Chief Minister Shivakumar.
Inspections covered petrol pumps as well as the ethanol blending and distribution stages of the supply chain.

stories.mainsQuestion: The rapid scale-up of ethanol blending in petrol is central to India's energy transition, yet it raises questions of fuel quality, consumer interest and food security. Examine these concerns in the light of recent State-level quality inspections, and suggest a regulatory way forward.

stories.headline: China factory-gate inflation fastest in nearly 4.5 years as consumer prices stay muted
stories.summary: China's producer price index rose in October at its fastest annual pace in nearly four-and-a-half years, indicating renewed cost pressure at the factory gate, while consumer price inflation moderated over the same month. The divergence suggests upstream input and commodity costs are building without a matching pass-through into retail prices, a pattern consistent with soft domestic demand in China. Wire and market reports framed the data as factory-gate inflation gaining momentum against muted consumer price pressures. For India, the reading matters chiefly through trade: China is a major source of intermediates, machinery and chemicals, so firmer factory-gate prices there can raise landed import costs and feed imported inflation into wholesale prices.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests the PPI-CPI distinction, the mechanics of imported inflation and the trade-offs facing inflation-targeting central banks — recurring GS-III economy and prelims themes.

perspectives.take: Global wire framing: data-led and neutral, leading on the multi-year high in factory-gate inflation while flagging the moderation in consumer prices as the second half of the story.

static.topic: Inflation Measurement: CPI, WPI and Producer Prices
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Inflation, Prices & Monetary Policy
static.whatIsIt: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level. India tracks retail prices through the Consumer Price Index (CPI) and wholesale prices through the Wholesale Price Index (WPI); a Producer Price Index (PPI) measures prices received by producers at the factory gate, excluding taxes and including services, and is the standard headline measure in economies such as China.
static.background: WPI has been published in India since the 1940s and is currently released by the Office of the Economic Adviser, DPIIT, with base year 2011-12, covering primary articles, fuel and power, and manufactured products. CPI (Combined) is compiled by the National Statistical Office with base year 2012, in which food and beverages carry the largest weight. Since 2016 the RBI's Monetary Policy Committee has targeted CPI inflation at 4% with a tolerance band of 2-6%, making CPI the operative headline measure. India has been discussing a shift towards a PPI framework to better capture producer-level price pressures.
static.socioEconomic: Food and fuel dominate the household inflation experience in India, so CPI and WPI frequently diverge; core inflation strips out these volatile components to reveal underlying pressure.
static.whyInNews: China's factory-gate (producer) inflation rose at its fastest pace in nearly four-and-a-half years in October even as consumer price inflation moderated — a PPI-CPI divergence that illustrates how upstream cost pressures may or may not pass through to retail prices.
static.wayForward: Strengthen the statistical architecture by developing a PPI alongside CPI, improve pass-through analysis, and keep monetary policy anchored to headline CPI while monitoring input-cost shocks.
prelimsPointers: India's WPI is released by the Office of the Economic Adviser (DPIIT); CPI (Combined) by the National Statistical Office.
The RBI's inflation target is 4% CPI with a 2-6% band, set under the 2016 amendment to the RBI Act.
China's CPI and PPI are published by its National Bureau of Statistics.
static.mainsAngle: Examine why producer and consumer inflation can diverge and what that implies for the credibility and conduct of inflation targeting in an open economy.

static.topic: Imported Inflation and India's Import Dependence on China
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — External Sector, Trade & Inflation
static.whatIsIt: Imported inflation arises when higher prices of imported goods — inputs, intermediates, capital goods or energy — raise domestic costs. China is one of India's largest sources of imports, especially electronics, machinery, chemicals, active pharmaceutical ingredients and intermediate goods, so price movements at China's factory gate can transmit into India's input costs and wholesale prices.
static.background: India's trade deficit with China has been persistently large, and industry bodies and official reviews have repeatedly flagged dependence on Chinese intermediates and active pharmaceutical ingredients. Policy responses have included production-linked incentives, phased manufacturing programmes and import-diversification efforts. Global supply-chain disruptions since 2020 have demonstrated how foreign producer-price shocks reach Indian firms.
static.geography: China's factory-gate prices are shaped by domestic industrial capacity, commodity input costs and export demand; India's exposure runs through ports, electronics clusters and pharmaceutical supply chains.
static.socioEconomic: Cheaper Chinese imports benefit consumers and downstream MSMEs but pressure domestic producers; costlier imports can feed into retail prices and widen the trade deficit.
static.whyInNews: Faster Chinese factory-gate inflation could raise the landed cost of Indian imports of intermediates and capital goods, feeding imported inflation even while domestic demand conditions remain soft.
static.wayForward: Diversify import sources, deepen domestic manufacturing of critical intermediates, monitor pass-through into WPI and CPI, and use trade remedies where dumping is established.
prelimsPointers: China is among India's largest import sources, with a large bilateral trade deficit.
Imported inflation typically shows up in WPI faster than in CPI because wholesale prices capture traded inputs more directly.
Anti-dumping and countervailing duties in India are administered through the Directorate General of Trade Remedies.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how India's import dependence on China transmits external price shocks, and evaluate the policy options available to cushion the domestic economy.

static.topic: Global Inflation Spillovers and Monetary Policy Divergence
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Monetary Policy & Global Economic Environment
static.whatIsIt: Inflation is increasingly synchronised across economies through commodity prices, shipping costs and supply chains. When major economies such as China, the United States or the European Union experience price shocks, emerging markets face imported cost pressures and difficult trade-offs between supporting growth and preserving price stability.
static.background: The 2021-23 global inflation episode, driven by pandemic-era supply disruptions and the energy shock following the war in Ukraine, forced aggressive rate tightening across advanced economies with spillovers into emerging-market currencies and capital flows. The RBI's MPC framework, with its 4% CPI target, was tested through this period.
static.socioEconomic: Emerging economies face a trilemma of exchange-rate stability, free capital flows and independent monetary policy; imported inflation sharpens this trade-off.
static.whyInNews: China's producer-price acceleration alongside muted consumer inflation adds to uncertainty about the global inflation path and the room available to central banks, including the RBI, for rate decisions.
static.wayForward: Maintain adequate forex reserves, use targeted fiscal measures for vulnerable households, strengthen domestic supply chains, and preserve central bank credibility through transparent communication.
prelimsPointers: The MPC has six members — three from the RBI including the Governor as chair, and three external members.
Repo is the rate at which the RBI lends to banks against securities; the reverse repo absorbs liquidity.
Inflation targeting was adopted through a 2016 amendment to the RBI Act.
static.mainsAngle: How should an inflation-targeting emerging economy respond to external price shocks without sacrificing growth? Illustrate with recent global experience.

prelims: China's factory-gate inflation is measured by the Producer Price Index, published along with CPI by its National Bureau of Statistics.
PPI tracks prices received by producers; CPI tracks retail prices paid by consumers — a PPI-CPI gap signals limited pass-through or weak demand.
In India, WPI is released by the Office of the Economic Adviser (DPIIT) and CPI by the NSO; the RBI targets CPI at 4% with a 2-6% band.
Imported inflation enters India mainly through intermediate goods, energy and capital goods imports.
stories.mainsQuestion: The divergence between producer and consumer price inflation in major economies complicates the inflation-targeting calculus for emerging economies like India. Discuss, with reference to imported inflation and India's trade linkages with China.

stories.headline: Ten years after demonetisation, cash remains king in India
stories.summary: On 8 November 2016, the Centre withdrew the legal tender status of ₹500 and ₹1,000 banknotes, pulling roughly 86% of the value of currency in circulation out of circulation overnight. A decade later, reporting on the anniversary records that cash continues to dominate everyday transactions in India despite the rapid expansion of digital payment channels such as UPI. The stated objectives — curbing black money, counterfeit notes and terror financing — are widely assessed as only partially met, with RBI disclosures indicating that almost all demonetised notes returned to the banking system. Digital payments have grown substantially in volume and value since, yet cash persists as the fallback medium for a large informal economy and for households with limited digital access.
stories.whyItMatters: Demonetisation is a standing case study in the GS-III economy syllabus on monetary policy, currency management and the informal sector, and its ten-year assessment ties directly to questions on digital payments, financial inclusion and the limits of supply-side policy shocks.

perspectives.take: Frames the ten-year anniversary as a verdict on the exercise's failure to dislodge cash, foregrounding the everyday persistence of cash usage; a South India-focused digital outlet, so the lens is on ordinary consumers and the regional everyday economy rather than macro policy design.

articles.title: Ten years after demonetisation, In India cash is still king

static.topic: Demonetisation of 2016 and Currency Management
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Monetary Policy, Currency and Banking
static.whatIsIt: The withdrawal of legal tender status of ₹500 and ₹1,000 banknotes announced on 8 November 2016, which overnight removed the bulk of the value of currency in circulation and forced a mass re-monetisation exercise through banks and post offices.
static.background: Announced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on 8 November 2016. The ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes together accounted for about 86% of the value of currency in circulation at the time. Stated objectives were to curb black money, counterfeit currency and terror financing, and to nudge the economy towards digital payments. The legal basis is Section 26(2) of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, under which the Centre may, on the recommendation of the RBI Central Board, declare that any series of banknotes shall cease to be legal tender. RBI's subsequent disclosures indicated that almost all the demonetised notes were returned to the banking system.
static.geography: India
static.socioEconomic: The exercise caused acute short-term disruption for cash-dependent households, small traders, daily-wage workers and the unorganised sector, while accelerating adoption of digital payment modes among formal-sector users. Its distributional effects fell disproportionately on those with the least access to banking and digital infrastructure.
static.whyInNews: The tenth anniversary of the 8 November 2016 announcement has revived public debate on whether the exercise met its objectives, with reporting noting that cash remains the dominant medium of transaction in India.
static.wayForward: Shift from one-off currency shocks to sustained institutional measures — strengthening financial inclusion, digital and offline payment infrastructure, cybersecurity, and targeted enforcement against black money and counterfeit currency.
prelimsPointers: Demonetisation was announced on 8 November 2016, withdrawing legal tender status of ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes.
The two denominations accounted for about 86% of the value of currency in circulation at the time.
Section 26(2) of the RBI Act, 1934 empowers the Centre to declare any series of banknotes as no longer legal tender, on the recommendation of the RBI Central Board.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate the outcomes of the 2016 demonetisation against its stated objectives, and assess what the persistence of cash a decade later reveals about the limits of currency-based policy interventions in an informal economy.

static.topic: Digital Payments Ecosystem and UPI
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Banking, Digital Payments and Financial Technology
static.whatIsIt: India's retail digital payment architecture, centred on the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) — a real-time, interoperable payment system that allows instant transfers between bank accounts through a single mobile interface.
static.background: The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) was set up in 2008 by the Reserve Bank of India and the Indian Banks' Association as an umbrella organisation for retail payments. UPI was launched in 2016, the same year as demonetisation, and the BHIM app followed in December 2016. Adoption expanded rapidly thereafter, with UPI becoming the dominant retail payment channel by volume. Other components include Aadhaar-enabled Payment System (AePS), IMPS, NEFT, RTGS and RuPay cards.
static.socioEconomic: Digital payments lower transaction costs, widen merchant acceptance and improve traceability, but adoption is uneven across income, age, gender and rural-urban divides. Concerns include cybersecurity, fraud, digital exclusion and the viability of the merchant discount rate regime for small merchants.
static.whyInNews: The tenth anniversary of demonetisation has focused attention on how far digital payments have displaced cash, with reporting indicating that cash continues to hold its ground despite UPI's expansion.
static.wayForward: Bridge the digital divide through offline and feature-phone payment modes, strengthen consumer protection and cybersecurity frameworks, and ensure digital payment growth is matched by last-mile financial inclusion.
prelimsPointers: UPI was launched in 2016 and is operated by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI).
NPCI was established in 2008 by the RBI and the Indian Banks' Association.
UPI enables real-time, interoperable bank-to-bank transfers through a single mobile interface.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether the expansion of digital payment infrastructure can by itself achieve a cashless economy, and examine the inclusion and security challenges that remain.

static.topic: Currency in Circulation and RBI's Currency Management
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Reserve Bank of India, Monetary Management and Currency
static.whatIsIt: The RBI's statutory function of issuing and managing banknotes, and the resulting stock of currency in circulation — a key indicator of the demand for cash in the economy.
static.background: Under Section 22 of the RBI Act, 1934, the RBI has the sole right to issue banknotes of all denominations except the one-rupee note, which is issued by the Government of India. Note issuance is backed by the minimum reserve system, under which the RBI maintains gold and foreign exchange reserves. The RBI follows a clean note policy and manages the denominational mix of notes in circulation. The ratio of currency in circulation to GDP is a commonly cited measure of the economy's reliance on cash.
static.socioEconomic: A high and rising currency-to-GDP ratio indicates continued dependence on cash for transactions and savings, particularly in the informal sector, and has implications for tax compliance, transaction traceability and the cost of currency management.
static.whyInNews: Ten years after demonetisation, commentary highlights that currency in circulation has continued to grow, underlining the resilience of cash demand.
static.wayForward: Improve the efficiency of currency logistics and note quality, while pursuing digital and financial inclusion so that the shift away from cash is driven by genuine convenience rather than coercion.
prelimsPointers: The RBI issues all banknotes except the one-rupee note, which is issued by the Government of India.
Note issuance by the RBI is governed by Section 22 of the RBI Act, 1934 and backed by the minimum reserve system.
The currency-to-GDP ratio is used as an indicator of the economy's reliance on cash.
static.mainsAngle: Examine why currency in circulation has continued to rise in India despite the growth of digital payments, and discuss the implications for monetary management and tax compliance.

prelims: Demonetisation was announced on 8 November 2016, withdrawing the legal tender status of ₹500 and ₹1,000 banknotes.
The ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes accounted for about 86% of the value of currency in circulation at the time of the announcement.
Under Section 26(2) of the RBI Act, 1934, the Centre can declare any series of banknotes to no longer be legal tender on the recommendation of the RBI Central Board.
UPI, launched in 2016, is a real-time retail payment system operated by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), which was set up in 2008.
stories.mainsQuestion: Ten years after demonetisation, cash continues to dominate Indian transactions even as digital payments expand rapidly. Critically examine whether the 2016 exercise achieved its stated objectives, and evaluate the role of digital payment infrastructure in shaping India's transition away from cash.

stories.headline: Hasina seeks new passport, signalling a possible return to Bangladesh
stories.summary: Ousted Bangladeshi prime minister Sheikh Hasina has applied for a fresh passport, according to an exclusive Reuters report republished by several international outlets — a step read as the clearest indication yet that she is preparing to return home. Hasina has been in India since she left office in August 2024 amid mass protests. Her legal position in Bangladesh remains contested, with proceedings pending against her, and the passport question touches on citizenship, travel documents and the terms of her stay in India. The report is attributed to unnamed sources and has not been officially confirmed by either government. The development is being watched closely in Delhi and Dhaka because it could reshape the political and diplomatic calculus between the two neighbours.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests India's balancing act between sheltering a former ally and managing ties with the government now in Dhaka, while raising live questions on extradition, asylum and the legal status of foreign nationals — recurring GS-II themes. The story also feeds directly into India's Neighbourhood First policy and the wider politics of South Asia.

perspectives.take: Breaks the story as an exclusive, framing the passport application as the 'clearest sign' of a planned return; wire-service register, attributed to unnamed sources with no official confirmation.
