static.topic: India–Bangladesh Relations
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its Neighbourhood
static.whatIsIt: The bilateral relationship between India and Bangladesh, covering a shared land border, trade and connectivity, water sharing, security cooperation and people-to-people ties, managed through a dense set of treaties and bilateral mechanisms.
static.background: Bangladesh became independent in 1971 with Indian military and diplomatic support, and India was among the first countries to recognise it. The relationship was institutionalised through the 1972 Indira–Mujib accord and the 1974 Land Boundary Agreement, the 1996 Ganga Waters Treaty, the 2013 Extradition Treaty and the 2015 operationalisation of the Land Boundary Agreement. Ties have fluctuated with changes of government in Dhaka, and the Teesta water-sharing issue remains unresolved.
static.geography: Bangladesh is bordered by India on three sides and by Myanmar on a short southeastern stretch, with the Bay of Bengal to the south. It shares boundaries with West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
static.socioEconomic: Bangladesh is among India's largest trading partners in South Asia, with strong links in textiles and garments, labour migration, remittances and cross-border connectivity projects. Border management, illegal migration and river water sharing are persistent socio-economic pressure points.
static.whyInNews: Reports that Sheikh Hasina has applied for a new passport have revived speculation about her return to Bangladesh and about the trajectory of India–Bangladesh ties.
static.wayForward: India needs to keep channels open with whichever government holds office in Dhaka, delink humanitarian and legal questions from political signalling, and push pending issues such as Teesta and connectivity projects through existing bilateral mechanisms.
prelimsPointers: India and Bangladesh share a border of about 4,096 km, the longest India shares with any neighbour.
The 2015 Land Boundary Agreement operationalised the 1974 pact and settled the exchange of enclaves and adverse possessions.
The Ganga Waters Treaty was signed in 1996; the Teesta sharing agreement is still pending.
static.mainsAngle: Political transitions in Bangladesh and their implications for India's Neighbourhood First policy, border management and regional connectivity.

static.topic: Extradition, Asylum and the Legal Status of Foreign Nationals
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — extradition and asylum; also relevant to GS-III internal security
static.whatIsIt: The domestic and treaty framework governing the surrender of accused persons between states, and the protection extended to foreign nationals present in India.
static.background: Extradition in India is governed by the Extradition Act, 1962, which works alongside bilateral treaties. India and Bangladesh signed an Extradition Treaty in 2013. India has no dedicated asylum or refugee law: foreign nationals are dealt with under the Foreigners Act, 1946 and executive discretion, and India is not a party to the 1951 UN Refugee Convention or its 1967 Protocol.
static.whyInNews: Questions about Hasina's travel documents and her continued stay in India bring extradition, asylum and the status of foreign nationals back into focus.
static.wayForward: India could consider a domestic asylum framework to bring predictability to cases involving foreign nationals, while continuing to rely on treaty-based extradition with defined exceptions.
prelimsPointers: The India–Bangladesh Extradition Treaty was signed in 2013 and allows refusal of extradition for offences of a political character.
India is not a signatory to the 1951 UN Refugee Convention or the 1967 Protocol.
A passport is a sovereign travel document; its issue, renewal or revocation is governed by a state's domestic law.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether India's reliance on executive discretion rather than a statutory asylum framework creates legal uncertainty for foreign nationals and diplomatic complications with neighbours.

static.topic: Regional Groupings and India's Neighbourhood Policy
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — regional groupings and India's neighbourhood
static.whatIsIt: The institutional architecture of South Asian and Bay of Bengal regionalism — SAARC, BIMSTEC and BBIN — through which India pursues connectivity, trade and political cooperation.
static.background: SAARC was founded in 1985 at Dhaka, with its secretariat in Kathmandu, but has been largely paralysed by India–Pakistan tensions. BIMSTEC, established by the 1997 Bangkok Declaration with its secretariat in Dhaka, has been positioned by India as a more workable alternative. BBIN, launched in 2015, focuses on sub-regional connectivity, including motor vehicles and grid connectivity.
static.geography: The Bay of Bengal littoral and the eastern South Asian landmass, spanning Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Myanmar and Thailand in the BIMSTEC format.
static.socioEconomic: Regional cooperation is tied to trade facilitation, energy grid interconnection, port and road connectivity, and disaster management across the Bay of Bengal region.
static.whyInNews: Political uncertainty in Bangladesh affects the functioning of SAARC, BIMSTEC and BBIN, several of whose secretariats and projects are anchored in Dhaka.
static.wayForward: India should insulate technical and connectivity cooperation from political turbulence, and continue to work through multiple regional formats so that progress does not depend on any single government.
prelimsPointers: SAARC was established in 1985 with its secretariat at Kathmandu; BIMSTEC was established in 1997 with its secretariat at Dhaka.
BBIN is a sub-regional initiative among Bangladesh, Bhutan, India and Nepal launched in 2015.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how political instability in a member state affects the credibility of regional groupings, and evaluate India's strategy of pursuing multiple regional formats in South Asia.

prelims: India and Bangladesh share a border of about 4,096 km, the longest India has with any neighbour.
The India–Bangladesh Extradition Treaty was signed in 2013 and permits refusal of extradition for offences of a political character.
India has no dedicated asylum law; foreign nationals are governed by the Foreigners Act, 1946, and India is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention.
A passport is a sovereign travel document, and its issue, renewal or revocation is a matter of a state's domestic law and executive discretion.
stories.mainsQuestion: Political turbulence in a neighbouring state inevitably spills over into India's diplomacy and security. In the light of recent developments in Bangladesh, examine the challenges such transitions pose to India's Neighbourhood First policy and suggest a way forward.

Gold rose over 1% as softer oil eased inflation worries, while Asian equities steadied as AI and Middle East jitters receded; investors awaited CPI data.

static.topic: RBI, monetary policy and the rupee-bond axis
static.syllabusNode: Indian Economy — Banking & Monetary Policy
static.whatIsIt: The RBI is India's central bank, established in 1935 and nationalised in 1949 under the RBI Act, 1934. It conducts monetary policy through the six-member Monetary Policy Committee, instituted in 2016 with a 4% CPI inflation target and a ±2% band.
static.background: The MPC framework came from the Urjit Patel Committee (2014) and a 2016 RBI Act amendment. Tools include repo/reverse repo, Marginal Standing Facility, Cash Reserve Ratio, Statutory Liquidity Ratio and Open Market Operations. The RBI also regulates banks, manages forex reserves and acts as banker to government.
static.socioEconomic: Soft crude oil and lower US Treasury yields can ease inflation and support bonds, while a firm dollar on Fed bets can cap rupee gains and influence capital flows.
static.whyInNews: The rupee and bond markets are firm on benign oil and lower Treasury yields, while dollar strength on Fed bets tests the rupee rally; CPI data is awaited.
static.wayForward: Watch CPI and Fed signals; the RBI's inflation-targeting framework guides liquidity and rate transmission amid global spillovers.
prelimsPointers: Repo is the rate at which RBI lends to banks against securities; reverse repo is the absorbing rate.
MPC has six members: three RBI members including the Governor as chair, plus three external members; the Governor has a casting vote.
Inflation target is 4% CPI with a 2-6% band, reviewed every five years.

static.background: Muhurat trading is a customary session on Diwali; Samvat refers to the Vikram Samvat calendar year. SEBI regulates intermediaries, disclosure and investor protection, while equity markets remain sensitive to global risk, oil and Fed expectations.

static.whyInNews: Samvat 2083 began with a tepid Muhurat session; benchmarks slipped while smaller companies and select NSE 500 stocks rose.

Muhurat trading is a customary Diwali session; Samvat is the Hindu calendar year.

stories.headline: Diwali night fires gut shops and homes in Mumbai, Hyderabad, Jammu and Katni
stories.summary: A cluster of fires over the Deepavali period gutted shops and homes in several Indian cities and killed at least six people. In Mumbai, a major blaze in Dongri was declared a Level-I fire call by the Mumbai Fire Brigade at 10.11 p.m., with fire, police, BEST, ward and ambulance teams deployed for dousing operations; a separate high-rise fire on November 7 had left one person dead. Hyderabad recorded a series of incidents at firecracker shops and godowns, including a blaze at a plastic manufacturing unit in Katedan Industrial Area that spread to an adjoining plywood unit and required three fire engines. In Jammu, a fire engulfed Nehru Market and gutted around twelve shops, while a store room at the Kathua district police lines also caught fire. In Madhya Pradesh, six members of a family were killed when a fire broke out at a crockery shop in a three-storey building in Barhi town in Katni district.
stories.whyItMatters: Recurrent festive-season fires test India's urban fire-safety regulation, municipal enforcement capacity and disaster-management architecture — core GS-III disaster management and GS-II urban governance themes.

perspectives.take: Frames the fires as a multi-city civic-safety failure, reporting municipal response detail (Mumbai's Level-I call, Hyderabad's three fire engines) and market-level losses in Jammu.

static.topic: Urban Fire Safety and Building Regulation in India
static.syllabusNode: Disaster Management — Urban Fire Safety and Building Regulations
static.whatIsIt: Fire safety in India is enforced mainly through State fire services and municipal building bye-laws, guided by the National Building Code of India (NBC) 2016 and the Model Building Bye-laws, 2016. NBC Part 4 lays down fire and life safety requirements — exits, compartmentation, sprinklers, alarms and fire-fighting installations — classified by building occupancy.
static.background: Fire services are primarily a State subject, with the Standing Fire Advisory Council under the Ministry of Home Affairs advising on standards and the National Fire Service College, Nagpur, training officers. The Model Building Bye-laws, 2016 (MoHUA) provide the template that States adopt for fire-safety clearances, while NBC 2016 (BIS) is the technical benchmark. Enforcement rests with municipal corporations and local bodies, which issue fire NOCs for occupancy.
static.socioEconomic: Rapid, often unplanned urbanisation, high-density commercial markets, mixed-use buildings and informal electrical wiring raise fire risk; small traders and slum households typically lack insurance and face total loss of livelihood after a blaze.
static.whyInNews: A cluster of Deepavali-period fires — Dongri in Mumbai, firecracker shops and godowns in Hyderabad, Nehru Market in Jammu, and a building in Katni — gutted shops and homes and killed six members of a family in Katni.
static.wayForward: Periodic third-party fire audits, digitised NOC renewal, mandatory sprinkler and alarm retrofits in high-density markets, dedicated fire lanes, and capacity expansion of municipal fire services with modern equipment and trained personnel.
prelimsPointers: NBC Part 4 deals with fire and life safety; the Code is published by the Bureau of Indian Standards.
Fire services are primarily a State subject; the National Fire Service College is located at Nagpur.
static.mainsAngle: Examine why fire-safety regulation remains weakly enforced in Indian cities and suggest institutional reforms to close the gap between codes and compliance.

static.topic: Disaster Management Framework in India
static.syllabusNode: Disaster Management — Institutional Framework
static.whatIsIt: The Disaster Management Act, 2005 created a three-tier institutional structure — NDMA at the national level, SDMAs in States and DDMAs in districts — supported by the NDRF, NIDM and NDMA guidelines.
static.background: The Act marked a shift from a relief-centric approach to preparedness and mitigation. NDMA is chaired by the Prime Minister, SDMA by the Chief Minister and DDMA by the District Magistrate. The NDRF was raised in 2006 as a specialised response force. Funding flows through the National and State Disaster Response Funds, with fire among the disasters listed for assistance.
static.socioEconomic: Fire losses fall hardest on uninsured small businesses and informal workers; compensation and rebuilding support depend on State relief norms and disaster-fund eligibility.
static.whyInNews: The Deepavali fires across four States have renewed focus on whether fire preparedness and response capacity match rising urban risk.
static.wayForward: Strengthen district-level fire risk mapping, integrate fire services into SDMA and DDMA plans, standardise fire-safety audits, and expand community-level first-response training.
prelimsPointers: NDMA is chaired by the Prime Minister; SDMA by the Chief Minister; DDMA by the District Magistrate.
The NDRF was constituted in 2006; fire is among the disasters eligible for State Disaster Response Fund assistance.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate whether India's disaster management architecture adequately addresses recurrent urban fire disasters, and suggest reforms.

static.topic: Firecracker Regulation and Green Crackers
static.syllabusNode: Environment & Governance — Firecracker Regulation and Air Pollution
static.whatIsIt: Manufacture, storage, sale and use of fireworks are regulated under the Explosives Act, 1884 and the Explosives Rules, 2008, administered by the Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation (PESO) under the DPIIT. The Supreme Court has separately restricted polluting crackers and mandated green crackers.
static.background: In Arjun Gopal v. Union of India (2018), the Supreme Court banned barium-based firecrackers and their online sale, permitted only green crackers developed by CSIR-NEERI, and fixed a limited bursting window on festivals. Sivakasi in Tamil Nadu is India's principal firecracker manufacturing cluster. States have since framed their own licensing and timing rules.
static.geography: Sivakasi in Tamil Nadu is the main fireworks manufacturing hub; firecracker godowns and retail shops are typically located in dense market areas, amplifying the risk of fire spread.
static.socioEconomic: The trade supports a large workforce in and around Sivakasi, while unlicensed storage in residential and market areas creates severe safety hazards for neighbouring households and traders.
static.whyInNews: A series of fire incidents at firecracker shops and godowns marred Deepavali in Hyderabad, alongside fires in Mumbai, Jammu and Katni.
static.wayForward: Strict licensing and inspection of storage godowns, separation of hazardous storage from dense markets, enforcement of green-cracker norms, and public awareness on safe storage and disposal.
prelimsPointers: PESO functions under the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT).
Green crackers were developed by CSIR-NEERI; the 2018 Supreme Court order banned barium-based firecrackers.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the balance between livelihood dependence on the firecracker industry and the imperatives of air quality and public safety.

prelims: Fire services are primarily a State subject; municipal corporations enforce fire safety through building bye-laws, with the National Building Code of India 2016 (Part 4) as the technical benchmark.
Under the Disaster Management Act, 2005, NDMA is chaired by the Prime Minister, SDMA by the Chief Minister and DDMA by the District Magistrate.
PESO, under the DPIIT, licenses the manufacture, storage and sale of fireworks under the Explosives Rules, 2008.
The Supreme Court in Arjun Gopal v. Union of India (2018) banned barium-based firecrackers and permitted only green crackers developed by CSIR-NEERI.
stories.mainsQuestion: Urban fire accidents recur every festive season, exposing gaps in regulation and enforcement. Examine the institutional and regulatory weaknesses in India's urban fire-safety framework and suggest measures to strengthen fire preparedness and response.
